pi.name: Andrzej Wierzbicki
pi.title: Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Andrzej Wierzbicki received his Ph.D. from the University of Warsaw, Poland, and was a postdoctoral research associate at Washington University in St. Louis before joining the University of Michigan faculty in 2009. His research asks how DNA is packaged and how that packaging relates to gene activity in the nucleus and in plastids, using plant experimental systems. He teaches genetics (BIO 305) and epigenetics (MCDB 462).

description: The Wierzbicki Lab studies how gene expression is regulated through chromatin structure and non-coding RNAs in plants. One major area is chloroplast chromatin: how chloroplast DNA is organized and packaged by nucleoid-associated proteins and how this packaging, including membrane association of active genes, connects to transcription by the plastid-encoded RNA polymerase. The second area is RNA-mediated transcriptional silencing, in which small interfering RNAs and long non-coding RNAs produced by the plant-specific polymerases Pol IV and Pol V direct DNA methylation, nucleosome positioning, and chromatin modifications that silence transposons and regulate genes. The lab works primarily in Arabidopsis thaliana, with additional work in maize, cucumber, and tomato, and combines mutant analysis, protein-RNA-DNA interaction assays, chromatin profiling, and high-throughput sequencing with bioinformatic analysis.

areas.title: Chloroplast chromatin
areas.summary: How chloroplast DNA is organized and packaged by nucleoid-associated proteins and how this packaging is connected to gene expression, studied with genetic tools in Arabidopsis, maize, cucumber, and tomato as the chloroplast equivalent of chromatin.

areas.title: RNA-mediated transcriptional silencing
areas.summary: How siRNAs and long non-coding RNAs cooperate to silence transposons and regulate genes through chromatin modifications, including how lncRNA production is regulated, how chromatin-modifying enzymes are recruited, and how nucleosome positioning and chromosome organization are controlled.
